## Simple explanation

System design is deciding how parts of a software system fit together to
meet user and operational needs. For an AI product, that includes the model,
data, APIs, storage, and the controls around them.

## Technical explanation

System design translates functional and non-functional requirements into
architecture, component responsibilities, interfaces, data flows, and
failure-handling strategies. AI-specific considerations include model
selection, inference capacity, evaluation, monitoring, privacy, and
fallback behavior.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

A useful model can still fail as a product if the surrounding system is
slow, unreliable, unsafe, or expensive. Explicit design makes trade-offs
visible and supports scaling, maintenance, and incident response.

## How it works

Engineers identify requirements and constraints, sketch components and
interactions, estimate capacity, and analyze failure modes. They validate
the design with prototypes, load tests, threat modeling, and operational
readiness checks, then revise it as evidence changes.

## Practical example

For a document question-answering service, design may include document
ingestion, access-aware retrieval, model inference, citations, rate limits,
and monitoring. Keeping retrieval separate from generation can help
diagnose poor answers and scale components independently.

## Common misconceptions

- System design is not only drawing boxes; interfaces, failure modes, and
  operational responsibilities must be specified.
- The most distributed or complex architecture is not automatically the
  best one; it should fit actual constraints.
